introduction.p: Before choosing a method, simplify the integrand and look for a derivative factor, a product suitable for integration by parts, a useful identity, or a rational expression suitable for partial fractions. No single technique works for every integral. We will compare these choices on examples.

subsection.title: Recognizing the structure of an integrand
subsection.p: A derivative rule leaves a fingerprint.
The chain rule often leaves a function and its derivative:
The product rule often leaves a product where one factor becomes simpler when differentiated:

p.me: x e^x, \qquad x\ln x, \qquad x\cos x.

subsection.p: Trigonometric identities appear when powers of sine, cosine, tangent, or secant are mixed:
Right-triangle identities appear when a square root has one of the forms
Partial fractions appear when the integrand is a rational function:
The first question is therefore not “What formula do I remember?” It is:

table.title: Recognizing the structure of an integrand

cell.p: A function together with something close to its derivative
Try substitution.
A product where one factor simplifies when differentiated
Try integration by parts.
Powers of trigonometric functions
Use trigonometric identities, then substitution.
A square root like a^2-x^2, a^2+x^2, or x^2-a^2
Try trigonometric substitution.
A quotient of polynomials
Use polynomial division if needed, then partial fractions.
A complicated expression that becomes simpler after expansion, factoring, or rationalizing
Do algebra before choosing a calculus method.

subsection.p: This table is a guide, not a law. Many integrals can be solved in more than one way. The best method is usually the one that reveals the structure most clearly.

exercise.title: Why is a technique a response to the shape of the integrand?

statement.p: A derivative rule leaves a fingerprint: a chain-rule pair, a product that simplifies when differentiated, a Pythagorean square root, a rational function. In your own words, why is the first question what structure do I see? rather than what formula do I remember??

hint.p: Each method undoes a specific kind of differentiation. Matching the method to the fingerprint is recognition, not a search through a bag of tricks.

subsection.title: Substitution first or parts first?
subsection.p: Some integrals look like products but are really substitution problems. Others look like they might have an inside function, but integration by parts is better.
A useful test is this:

p.me: \text{Before using parts, check whether substitution removes the whole problem.}

subsection.p: Integration by parts creates a new integral. Substitution often turns the integral directly into a known form. So substitution is usually the first thing to test.

exercise.title: Why test substitution before integration by parts?

statement.p: The product x e^{x^2} looks like a candidate for parts, but substitution removes the whole problem. In your own words, why is substitution usually the first thing to test, and what is the difference between a product that is really a chain rule and a product that really needs parts?

hint.p: Substitution often turns the integral directly into a known form. Parts always creates a new integral. Check whether the inside function’s derivative is already present.

note.p: When both seem possible, try substitution first. If it does not simplify the integral, look for parts.

subsection.title: Algebraic simplification
subsection.p: Sometimes the right technique is hidden behind algebra. Before reaching for a new calculus method, simplify the integrand.
Algebra can reveal substitution, partial fractions, cancellation, or a known form.

exercise.title: Why can algebra be the real technique?

statement.p: Dividing, canceling, completing the square, or expanding can reveal a simple integrand that was hiding. In your own words, why should you simplify before reaching for a new calculus method, and what does that say about where the difficulty often lives?

hint.p: Many hard-looking integrals are easy after a rewrite. The calculus step is then a basic formula; the work was algebraic recognition.

subsection.title: When no elementary antiderivative exists
subsection.p: It is natural to hope that every continuous function has a familiar antiderivative. The Fundamental Theorem tells us that every continuous function f has an antiderivative:
But it does not say that F can be written using the elementary functions we already know.

By elementary functions, we mean functions built from polynomials, rational functions, powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, inverse trigonometric functions, and combinations of these by addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and composition.
Many elementary functions have antiderivatives that are not elementary.
Famous examples include
and
This is not a failure of calculus. It is a sign that the family of elementary functions is not closed under antidifferentiation.

paragraphs.title: The Gaussian example
paragraphs.p: is a perfectly good function, and the Fundamental Theorem gives
But G(x) cannot be expressed using elementary functions. So instead of forcing it into old language, mathematicians name it. A scaled version is called the error function:
The name is not a trick. It is a recognition that this accumulation is important enough to become a function in its own right.

paragraphs.title: A definite integral may still be meaningful
paragraphs.p: has no elementary antiderivative, the definite integral
still has a definite value. It measures accumulated area. We can approximate it numerically. Later, we will also approximate it with power series.
The absence of an elementary antiderivative does not stop the integral from existing.

p.em: Exact elementary formulas are useful, but they are not the only way to know an integral.

exercise.title: Why can an antiderivative exist without being elementary?

statement.p: Part I guarantees that every continuous function has an antiderivative F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt. In your own words, why does that not mean F can be written from polynomials, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions, and why is that not a failure of calculus?

hint.p: The family of elementary functions is not closed under antidifferentiation. The accumulation function is still a genuine function; it may simply be a new name, such as the error function, or a quantity we approximate.

subsection.title: Strategy summary
subsection.p: Integration is less mechanical than differentiation. Differentiation has a direct rule for each way of building a function. Integration asks us to recognize what construction might have produced the integrand.
A useful final checklist is:

cell.p: Can the integrand be simplified algebraically?
Factor, cancel, expand, rationalize, complete the square, or divide.
Is there an inside function with its derivative nearby?
Use substitution.
Is there a product with a factor that simplifies under differentiation?
Use integration by parts.
Are there trigonometric powers or products?
Use identities and then substitute.
Is there a square root matching a Pythagorean pattern?
Use trigonometric or hyperbolic substitution.
Is the integrand rational?
Use polynomial division and partial fractions.
Is it a definite integral with symmetry or geometry?
Use the bounds and the shape before seeking an antiderivative.
Does no elementary method work?
Define a new accumulation function, approximate numerically, or use series.

subsection.p: The best way to learn strategy is to practice with mixed examples. But the guiding principle stays simple:

p.me: \text{Do not ask first, ``What technique should I use?''}

subsection.p: Ask instead:

p.me: \text{What is the integrand trying to tell me?}

subsection.p: The next section adds a modern tool. Computer algebra systems and integral tables can find many antiderivatives. But they do not remove the need for thought. They make checking, interpretation, and domain awareness more important.
